Institutional brokers faced the immense challenge of "fragmentation"—a dynamic where 
liquidity was spread across over 30 distinct crossing systems.1 
The BATS Trading Acquisition and Strategic Opacity 
In September 2006, under Bleich's strategic guidance, Lehman Brothers formally announced 
that it had acquired a minority stake in BATS Trading (an acronym for Better Alternative Trading 
System).1 BATS was an emerging ECN founded in June 2005 by Dave Cummings, a pioneer in 
high-speed algorithmic trading who had previously established the automated liquidity 
provider Tradebot Systems.1 The BATS platform was explicitly designed as a next-generation 
matching engine capable of handling high-speed, high-volume, and anonymous algorithmic 
trading, catering specifically to high-frequency trading (HFT) firms by offering sub-millisecond 
latency execution and aggressive maker-taker pricing models.1 
At the time of the transaction, Bleich publicly championed the venue, stating that Lehman 
Brothers was "very excited" to announce the investment.1 He praised BATS for its emergence as 
a "thought leader, innovator and technology provider in the execution platform space".1 Bleich 
explicitly stated to the financial press that fragmentation was the core problem brokers needed 
to solve, advocating for the connection of dark liquidity pools because the fragmented trading 
environment made it difficult for institutional investors to execute large block trades without 
suffering "information leakage".1 
The SEC Enforcement Action and Whistleblower Revelations 
While Bleich's strategic mandate was ostensibly to secure efficient liquidity for Lehman's clients, 
the venue he aggressively capitalized and championed soon became the focal point of one of 
the most severe market structure scandals in modern history.1 The rapid ascent of BATS 
Trading—and its subsequent merger with Direct Edge Holdings to become the second-largest 
financial exchange in the country—was ultimately revealed to be built upon a foundation of 
structural deception catering almost exclusively to predatory HFT firms.1 
The SEC launched an aggressive, multi-year investigation into the practices of these 
high-frequency trading venues, propelled largely by the testimony, technical documents, and 
structural maps provided by whistleblower Haim Bodek.1 Bodek, a market structure expert and 
algorithmic designer, exposed how financial exchanges were secretly rigging the market 
against traditional institutional and retail investors.1 
The SEC investigation conclusively revealed that Direct Edge and BATS had fundamentally 
deceived the investing public by creating secretive, highly complex order types—specifically 
variations of a routing process known as "price sliding".1 The exchanges offered three distinct 
variations of these order types but purposefully failed to accurately describe or disclose these
